notes: Remote runners use high-entropy runner secrets and dispatch tokens over TLS, but Journeyman does not currently use replay-resistant public-key mutual authentication such as mTLS between services.

All known backend/helper boundaries have finite timeouts and documented retry budgets; Git/helper gaps are now bounded, LDAP failover is one attempt per enabled server, and cleanup/failure behaviour is documented and regression tested.

Journeyman documents explicit lifecycles for break-glass access, API tokens, session-signing keys, credential-encryption keys, Signal Source HMAC secrets, remote-system credentials, and one-time runner/bootstrap secrets, with automated verification of the enforceable lifecycle rules.

Remote runners use per-runner authentication and database/external services require credentials, but Journeyman still supports long-lived service credentials rather than universally using short-term or certificate-based authentication.
Packaged services run under the dedicated journeyman account and deployment guidance requires least-privilege backend accounts; exact external-service privileges remain deployment-specific.

Journeyman ships no working default credentials for backend services. External credentials are administrator supplied; documented secret placeholders are not accepted as the production session-signing secret.
Production administrator-configured Git, inventory and environment-build proxy destinations are constrained by JOURNEYMAN_OUTBOUND_ALLOWED_HOSTS, which is owned outside the web UI.
Packaged ProductionConfig enforces the outbound destination allowlist at application validation and runtime request boundaries.
Backend-specific timeouts exist, but connection-pool limits, saturation behaviour and retry strategies are not yet uniformly documented and enforced for every separate service.
Journeyman encrypts stored secrets with an external file-backed key but does not yet integrate with a dedicated secrets-management solution or hardware-backed vault/HSM.
Secret key material is permission-restricted and application secret reveal is subject to least-privilege authorization.
Cryptographic operations currently execute in the Journeyman process using file-backed key material rather than an isolated HSM/security module.

Journeyman hard-expires break-glass access and API tokens, automatically rotates the session-signing key on eligible boots, warns administrators before or at rotation deadlines for encryption/HMAC secrets, and flags externally managed credentials for policy review without causing an availability-breaking local expiry.
The supported release archive builder excludes .git metadata, runtime instance data, virtual environments, caches, logs, bytecode, and built tarballs; regression tests verify the exclusion boundary.
Packaged production service configuration explicitly selects ProductionConfig, which disables debug mode; the development entry point no longer forces debug on.
The managed production Nginx configuration explicitly disables directory indexing with autoindex off.
The application does not expose TRACE routes; regression coverage requires HTTP TRACE to return Method Not Allowed.
Administrative monitoring/status information is intentionally exposed only through authorization-protected application endpoints; project documentation is not served as a web route.
Application responses are checked not to advertise Python, Flask, Werkzeug or Gunicorn versions in response headers. Journeyman intentionally displays its own application version.
A strict reverse-proxy allowlist of servable file extensions is not currently enforced by Journeyman deployment configuration.
Sensitive Journeyman data is classified into restricted secrets, protected operational data and ordinary metadata.
Protection requirements cover encryption, logging, access control, transport placement, caching and retention expectations.
Runner API and dispatch secrets are carried in headers; credential/package secrets are submitted in request bodies, not documented URL/query parameters.
Server-side inventory caches have bounded retention and protected application records are purged according to the configured retention policy.
Journeyman templates do not load common third-party analytics/tracking services that would receive application data.
Protected data now has explicit retention, purge, authenticated no-store caching, encryption/access-control, and deployment backup-retention requirements.
Journeyman does not intentionally provide a shared application cache, but end-to-end Web Cache Deception hardening across deployment reverse proxies has not yet been verified.
Credential values are masked by default and full recoverable values are returned only through an explicit owner-authorized reveal operation.
Terminal Job evidence and dependent sensitive snapshots/outputs are automatically purged after the configured retention period.
Journeyman currently has no general end-user file-upload feature whose submitted metadata is retained.
Logout clears the authenticated session and Journeyman application code does not use localStorage/sessionStorage/IndexedDB for sensitive state.
All authenticated application responses receive no-store/no-cache headers centrally.

Journeyman does not use localStorage/sessionStorage/IndexedDB, but the signed Flask client-side session cookie can contain authenticated identity/session metadata and is integrity-protected rather than encrypted.
Risk-based third-party remediation targets are documented.

Each release generates a version-bound SHA-256 source manifest and SPDX 2.3 SBOM from the exact production dependency lock, including direct and transitive Python components. The manifest records the dependency-lock digest and can verify installed release files for post-install modification; signing is performed with a maintainer-controlled release key outside production.
Resource-demanding functionality and queue/concurrency/timeout defenses are documented.
Risky third-party components are identified for additional review.
Dangerous functionality such as shell, Ansible, Git, runner bootstrap, and secret reveal is explicitly documented.

The maintainer must audit every supported release dependency lock with pip-audit at least weekly and before release. Applicable findings require remediation, complete regression/security testing, regenerated lock/SBOM/provenance, and a new maintenance release; non-applicable or deferred findings require an explicit documented security exception.
Project and runner execution capacity is bounded and queued work is atomically claimed.
Production configuration disables debug/development functionality and the packaged service pins ProductionConfig.
A transitive dependency lock/SBOM with cryptographic provenance and dependency-confusion prevention is not yet enforced by Journeyman release tooling.
Dangerous functionality has authorization and OS/service boundaries but is not generally sandboxed or separately containerized as required for this Level-3 control.
Security-sensitive responses/manifests use explicit field subsets rather than whole ORM object serialization.
Git, Zabbix, and delegated Satellite/Foreman HTTP paths explicitly reject redirects; the Foreman subprocess receives a scoped Requests no-redirect guard.
Controllers explicitly extract allowed request fields; bulk request-dictionary mass assignment is prohibited by regression test.
Production ProxyFix trusts exactly one proxy hop and application code does not consume X-Forwarded-For directly.
Security-sensitive inputs frequently perform explicit conversion/range checks, but Python is dynamically typed and universal strict type/comparator verification has not been demonstrated.
Journeyman does not accept or merge attacker-controlled JavaScript object graphs; no client-side object-merging/prototype-extension facility is used as an application data model.
Journeyman rejects duplicate scalar query/form parameters before route handling while explicitly allowing only known multi-value form fields.
Journeyman coordinates core execution state through the database, but a complete review proving thread safety for every shared in-process/file resource has not been completed.
Atomic conditional database claims are used for runner work, but universal TOCTOU safety across filesystem and database check/action pairs has not been demonstrated.
Journeyman does not implement application-managed thread lock graphs; coordination is primarily database/process based. Reassess if explicit threaded locking is introduced.
Gunicorn/process and runner concurrency limits exist, but Journeyman does not implement or verify a Level-3 fair thread scheduling policy.
The logging inventory documents the structured audit log, operational application logs, recorded metadata, access controls, storage expectations and known retention/centralization gaps.
Structured audit events retain timestamp, actor, authentication mechanism, action/result, object metadata, source IP and request correlation identifier.
Audit timestamps are generated in UTC, but Journeyman does not currently verify time synchronization across the application host, database, runners and external systems.
The documented logging inventory identifies the database audit log and operational application/service logging channels used by Journeyman.
The database audit log is structured, but Journeyman does not yet mandate one common parseable format and processor for all operational logs.
Audit detail keys associated with passwords, secrets, tokens, credentials, authorization, cookies and CSRF values are redacted before persistence.
Successful and failed interactive authentication attempts are persisted with result and authentication mechanism metadata.
HTTP 403 authorization failures are captured centrally as authorization.denied audit events without request-body contents.
Central rejection auditing records validation, conflict, and anti-automation failures while specific authentication/CSRF/authorization events remain available.
Security-control/backend authentication failures and unhandled exceptions are classified and represented in the audit trail.
Structured audit JSON plus an application logging filter prevents CR/LF-controlled text from forging conventional log lines.
Audit viewing is administrator-only and no mutation route exists, but database-level append-only or tamper-evident enforcement is not yet implemented.
Journeyman does not yet require secure forwarding of security logs to a logically separate SIEM/logging system.
Unexpected server exceptions produce a generic HTTP 500 response while detailed exception information remains server-side.
Several dependency failures fail closed, but Journeyman does not yet provide or verify a uniform circuit-breaker/graceful-degradation policy for all external resources.
Application security boundaries were reviewed for fail-closed behavior; representative automated regression tests are referenced by the review.
A last-resort application HTTP 500 handler returns a controlled response and records unhandled exception details server-side.
